Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition

Watch the second player mix two strategies by probability. Slide the mixing probability back and forth.

As the rival's mix changes, my expected payoff from each strategy moves along a straight line. At the mix where the two lines cross, neither strategy is better. Only that indifferent mix can appear in a mixed equilibrium. Making your rival indifferent is what pins down your mix.

For example, say a 🧑 friend takes a penalty kick with a ⚽ ball against a goalkeeper friend. Always kicking left lets the keeper guard only left. So the kicker mixes left and right kicks. The mix makes the keeper equally unhappy guarding either side.

u1(Top,q)=q uTL+(1−q) uTRu_1(\text{Top}, q) = q\,u_{TL} + (1-q)\,u_{TR}u1​(Top,q)=quTL​+(1−q)uTR​
q∗:u1(Top,q∗)=u1(Bottom,q∗)q^* : u_1(\text{Top}, q^*) = u_1(\text{Bottom}, q^*)q∗:u1​(Top,q∗)=u1​(Bottom,q∗)

Examples & Exercises

In Matching Pennies, find the mix q∗q^*q∗ of player 2 that makes player 1 indifferent, and explain why.

u1(H,q)=q⋅1+(1−q)⋅(−1)=2q−1u_1(H, q) = q \cdot 1 + (1-q) \cdot (-1) = 2q - 1u1​(H,q)=q⋅1+(1−q)⋅(−1)=2q−1
u1(T,q)=q⋅(−1)+(1−q)⋅1=1−2qu_1(T, q) = q \cdot (-1) + (1-q) \cdot 1 = 1 - 2qu1​(T,q)=q⋅(−1)+(1−q)⋅1=1−2q
Show proof

  1. Let player 2 play HHH with probability qqq.

    Player 1's expected payoff from HHH is 2q−12q - 12q−1, from TTT is 1−2q1 - 2q1−2q.

    The indifference condition 2q−1=1−2q2q - 1 = 1 - 2q2q−1=1−2q gives q∗=1/2q^* = 1/2q∗=1/2.

  2. The key insight: in a mixed equilibrium each player chooses the mix that "makes the opponent indifferent" — not the mix maximizing their own payoff, but the one giving the opponent the incentive to mix.

    If q<1/2q < 1/2q<1/2, TTT is better (1−2q>2q−11-2q > 2q-11−2q>2q−1); if q>1/2q > 1/2q>1/2, HHH is better.

    Only at q∗q^*q∗ is every mix of player 1 (weakly) optimal.

In the Battle of the Sexes, find q∗q^*q∗ making player 1 indifferent and p∗p^*p∗ making player 2 indifferent.

u1(O,q)=3q,u1(F,q)=2(1−q)u_1(O, q) = 3q, \qquad u_1(F, q) = 2(1-q)u1​(O,q)=3q,u1​(F,q)=2(1−q)
u2(p,O)=2p,u2(p,F)=3(1−p)u_2(p, O) = 2p, \qquad u_2(p, F) = 3(1-p)u2​(p,O)=2p,u2​(p,F)=3(1−p)
Show proof

  1. Player 1: u1(O,q)=3qu_1(O,q) = 3qu1​(O,q)=3q, u1(F,q)=2(1−q)u_1(F,q) = 2(1-q)u1​(F,q)=2(1−q). From 3q=2−2q3q = 2 - 2q3q=2−2q, q∗=2/5=0.4q^* = 2/5 = 0.4q∗=2/5=0.4.

    Player 2: u2(p,O)=2pu_2(p,O) = 2pu2​(p,O)=2p, u2(p,F)=3(1−p)u_2(p,F) = 3(1-p)u2​(p,F)=3(1−p). From 2p=3−3p2p = 3 - 3p2p=3−3p, p∗=3/5=0.6p^* = 3/5 = 0.6p∗=3/5=0.6.

  2. The fully mixed Nash equilibrium is (p∗,q∗)=(0.6,0.4)(p^*, q^*) = (0.6, 0.4)(p∗,q∗)=(0.6,0.4).

    Expected payoffs are 3×0.4=1.23 \times 0.4 = 1.23×0.4=1.2 for player 1 and 2×0.6=1.22 \times 0.6 = 1.22×0.6=1.2 for player 2 — worse for both than either pure equilibrium (3,2)(3,2)(3,2) or (2,3)(2,3)(2,3).

    Mixed equilibria can be Pareto inferior.
